1. FIRST-PRINCIPLES MODEL: WHY A BACTERIUM GROWS IN A FOOD
A source of carbon, nitrogen, minerals and growth factors.
An aqueous environment with a particular water activity.
A chemical environment defined by pH, buffering capacity and antimicrobial compounds.
A redox environment influenced by oxygen diffusion, packaging and microbial metabolism.
A physical structure containing surfaces, pores, fat droplets, particles and protected microenvironments.
Microbial behaviour follows from the interaction:
A species name alone does not determine risk.
Salmonella may survive in a dry food without multiplying.
Listeria monocytogenes may multiply slowly during refrigeration.
Clostridium perfringens spores may survive cooking and subsequently germinate during slow cooling.
Staphylococcus aureus cells may be killed by heating after enterotoxin has already accumulated.
Bacillus cereus spores may survive cooking, while the outcome depends on whether the strain produces enterotoxins or cereulide.

B. Corynebacterium diphtheriae: A–B toxin architecture

C. diphtheriae is primarily a pathogen of respiratory or cutaneous infection, not a standard cause of classical food-borne intoxication. Its inclusion is valuable for bacterial physiology and toxin-mechanism questions.
The toxin gene is associated with a toxigenic bacteriophage.
Not all C. diphtheriae isolates produce diphtheria toxin.
Iron availability regulates toxin expression through the DtxR regulatory system.
Iron limitation can permit toxin expression in a toxigenic strain.
Diphtheria toxin is produced as a polypeptide that can be proteolytically nicked into functional fragments held together by a disulphide linkage.
Fragment B binds the appropriate host-cell receptor.
The toxin enters by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
Fragment A uses NAD⁺ to ADP-ribosylate elongation factor 2.
The modified site is the diphthamide residue of eEF2.

[HPSC EXAM TRAP]
- A = active/catalytic; B = binding/translocation.
- Diphtheria toxin modifies eEF2, not bacterial EF-Tu.
- It does not act by the same ribosomal depurination mechanism as Shiga toxin.
- The presence of a species does not establish the presence or expression of its toxin gene.
First-principles model: cooking selects spores, while slow cooling permits explosive growth
Large meat masses cool unevenly. The exterior may cool while the interior remains within a favourable growth range. Cooking can remove competitors while leaving spores able to germinate.
Relatively aerotolerant compared with some strict anaerobes.

This is why warm holding and slow cooling of meat dishes are critical.
The combination of substantial food mass, surviving spores and poor cooling is more important than a particular recipe name.
A. Historical type A versus modern type F
Older food-microbiology texts identify ordinary food poisoning with type A strains.
The expanded toxinotyping system separates enterotoxigenic strains producing alpha toxin and CPE, but lacking the defining beta, epsilon and iota toxins, into type F.
Classical C. perfringens food poisoning was historically associated with enterotoxigenic type A strains; many such strains are classified as type F in the expanded scheme.
Not every historical type A strain carries the enterotoxin gene.
CPE is a protein of approximately 35 kDa.
Expression is strongly associated with sporulation.
In classical food poisoning, sporulation occurs in the intestine.
Toxin is released as the mother cell lyses.
Epithelial injury and altered intestinal fluid handling produce diarrhoea.
CPE is therefore a pore-forming enterotoxin.
Onset usually within approximately 6–24 hours, often around 8–16 hours.
Fever and vomiting are not usually dominant.
Illness is commonly self-limiting, but severe outcomes can occur.

Beta toxin is associated particularly with type C disease and necrotic enteritis.

blocks.text: [HPSC EXAM TRAP] Mould growth, visible mould, toxin production and toxin persistence are four different propositions.
1. FIRST-PRINCIPLES MODEL: WHY MOULDS GROW AND WHY MYCOTOXINS APPEAR

Filamentous fungi are favoured where oxygen is available, bacterial growth is restricted by low pH or low aw, substrates are rich in carbohydrates or lipids, and storage is warm, humid or poorly ventilated.
Spore deposition → germination → hyphal extension → mycelial colonisation → sporulation and/or toxin production
Growth does not imply toxin production in every strain.
Absence of visible growth does not imply absence of toxin.
Mould spoilage may cause visible mycelium, pigmentation, softening, dehydration, musty odours, lipolysis, pectin degradation and structural collapse.
Mycotoxigenesis is the formation of biologically active secondary metabolites by selected fungal strains under particular environmental and nutritional conditions.
Mycotoxin risk = f(toxigenic strain, aw, temperature, oxygen, substrate, time, stress and competition)

Primary metabolism supports growth, energy generation, biosynthesis and reproduction. Secondary metabolism produces compounds not essential for immediate biomass formation but potentially important in ecological competition, defence or stress responses.
Many mycotoxins are secondary metabolites. Their formation may increase during drought stress, insect damage, nutrient limitation, temperature shifts or microbial competition.
[HPSC EXAM TRAP] Secondary metabolite does not mean unimportant; it means not directly required for basic multiplication under ordinary conditions.
2. MORPHOLOGY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF FOOD MOULDS
A hypha is a tubular fungal filament. A network of hyphae forms a mycelium. Hyphae may be septate or sparsely septate depending on the group. Growth occurs mainly at the hyphal tip.
Tip growth requires membrane synthesis, cell-wall assembly, vesicle trafficking and polarised cytoskeletal transport. This enables moulds to penetrate cracks, pores and damaged plant tissue.
The common asexual spores of Aspergillus and Penicillium are conidia. They are produced externally on specialised structures, assist dissemination, and often tolerate drying.

Some food moulds produce sexual spores such as ascospores. These may be more heat-resistant than vegetative hyphae or conidia in certain species. A sexual stage is not required for spoilage or mycotoxin production.
Foot cell → conidiophore → vesicle → phialides → conidia
Species differ in stalk morphology, vesicle size, phialide arrangement, conidial colour and sclerotium formation.
The conidiophore branches into a brush-like penicillus containing branches, metulae, phialides and conidia. Arrangements may be monoverticillate, biverticillate or more complex.
[HPSC EXAM TRAP] The brush-like conidiophore is characteristic of Penicillium. Aspergillus typically forms a vesicle-based conidial head.
3. WATER ACTIVITY, OXYGEN AND MOULD GROWTH
where p is the vapour pressure of water above the food and p0 is the vapour pressure of pure water at the same temperature.
Therefore, aw = 0.80 corresponds approximately to 80% equilibrium relative humidity.
Total moisture percentage is insufficient because water may be bound to proteins, salts, sugars or the food matrix. Microorganisms respond more directly to available water than to total moisture.

Food-associated filamentous moulds are generally obligately aerobic. They are favoured by oxygenated surfaces, headspace oxygen, cracks, insect channels and inadequately sealed packages.
Vacuum packaging can suppress mould growth only if oxygen is sufficiently removed and maintained at a low level. Leaks, oxygen ingress or surface exposure can restore the aerobic niche.
Reduced oxygen may inhibit moulds but select for yeasts or anaerobic bacteria. It changes the hazard profile rather than eliminating all hazards.
Each species has minimum, optimum and maximum growth temperatures. The optimum for toxin production may differ from the optimum for biomass formation.

Fungal growth and many oxidative biosynthetic reactions require oxygen. Oxygen limitation may reduce hyphal growth, sporulation and toxin biosynthesis. Oxygen may nevertheless vary greatly within a food particle or package.

Mycotoxin production depends on carbon source, nitrogen source, lipids, trace minerals, plant defence compounds and available precursors. A substrate that supports growth does not necessarily support the same toxin profile.

Pre-harvest risk factors include drought, high temperature, insect feeding, plant disease, delayed harvest and mechanical injury. Damaged kernels permit easier fungal penetration and provide more available nutrients.

Rapid drying + uniform moisture + cool, clean storage + lot monitoring

A. flavus and A. parasiticus belong to Aspergillus section Flavi.
A. flavus commonly produces B-series aflatoxins. A. parasiticus commonly produces B- and G-series aflatoxins. Some section Flavi species also produce aflatoxins, and many strains are non-toxigenic.

The pathway is controlled by a biosynthetic gene cluster containing genes for polyketide synthesis, oxidation, reduction, methylation, transport and regulation.

The terminal 8,9 double bond in the terminal furan ring is central to this activation.
